title: Hemoglobin Measurement: the HiCN Method, Turbidity and Specimen Source
summary: Learn how the cyanmethemoglobin (HiCN) reference method measures hemoglobin, why lipemia, extreme leukocytosis and paraproteins falsely raise it, how to catch and correct the artefact, and how capillary and venous hemoglobin really compare.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 31 Hit 2 (HiCN reference method), Exam Trap 2 (falsely high HiCN absorbance) and Hit 12 (capillary vs venous Hb). HiCN chemistry from Garcia-Casal 2023 and Girard 2025 (GFHC); interferences from Girard 2025, Fan 2026 and Henry 2022; capillary vs venous from Neufeld 2019 and Krleza 2015. Hit 12 is contradicted (register flag rv-capillary-venous-hb-gap): open studies report capillary–venous Hb differences mostly of about 1 g/dL or less, in either direction, not ~3 g/dL; the RBC ~0.5 ×10¹²/L figure is not taught. Trap 2’s “WBC >30 ×10⁹/L” threshold is not taught (register flag rv-hicn-wbc-threshold): sources describe major hyperleukocytosis with no single cut-off.

objectives: Describe the HiCN reaction, the 540 nm reading and the hemoglobin derivative it does not convert.
Explain how lipemia, extreme leukocytosis and paraproteins falsely raise photometric hemoglobin and the calculated indices.
Detect and correct a turbidity artefact, and interpret capillary versus venous hemoglobin differences.

scenes.title: Two hemoglobins that do not add up
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: two hemoglobin results reach the bench. (1) A milky, lipemic EDTA sample from a patient receiving an intravenous lipid infusion: Hb 19.5 g/dL, Hct 39%, MCHC 50 g/dL. (2) A finger-stick Hb of 12.6 g/dL on a point-of-care device, and a venous Hb of 12.0 g/dL on the analyzer, drawn the same morning. Question token: “Real hemoglobin, or the measurement?”

cues.text: Two hemoglobin results reach the bench. The first is a milky sample from a patient on a lipid infusion: hemoglobin nineteen point five, but a hematocrit of only thirty-nine percent.
The second patient has a finger-stick hemoglobin of twelve point six, and a venous hemoglobin of twelve point zero from the same morning.
Is either difference real hemoglobin, or is it the measurement?

scenes.title: The cyanmethemoglobin reference method
scenes.altText: Schematic reaction chain: whole blood + Drabkin’s solution (potassium cyanide, potassium ferricyanide, potassium dihydrogen phosphate) → red cells lyse → ferricyanide oxidises hemoglobin to methemoglobin → cyanide binds to form hemiglobincyanide (HiCN, cyanmethemoglobin) → absorbance read at 540 nm and compared with an HiCN standard. Converted: oxyhemoglobin, methemoglobin, carboxyhemoglobin. Not converted: sulfhemoglobin. Side card: ICSH reference method; cyanide is toxic, so some analyzers use cyanide-free reagents such as sodium lauryl sulfate.

cues.text: The reference method for hemoglobin is cyanmethemoglobin, recommended by the International Committee for Standardization in Hematology. Blood is mixed with Drabkin’s solution: potassium cyanide, potassium ferricyanide and a phosphate salt.
The red cells lyse. Ferricyanide oxidises hemoglobin to methemoglobin, and cyanide then binds it to form hemiglobincyanide, also called cyanmethemoglobin.

The absorbance is read at five hundred forty nanometres and compared with a hemiglobincyanide standard. Oxy-, met- and carboxyhemoglobin are all converted, but sulfhemoglobin is not, so this method does not measure it.
Because cyanide is toxic, some automated analyzers use cyanide-free reagents such as sodium lauryl sulfate, but the reading is still a light-absorbance measurement.

scenes.title: Anything that clouds the lysate reads as hemoglobin
scenes.altText: Schematic cuvette: light at 540 nm passes through the lysate; extra particles scatter or absorb light, so absorbance rises and hemoglobin is overestimated. Interference cards: lipemia (severe hypertriglyceridemia, intravenous lipid emulsions); major hyperleukocytosis with large granular cells (CML, AML) whose lysed contents raise Hb; abundant monoclonal IgM or cryoglobulins that precipitate with some reagents even when plasma looks clear; icteric or haemolysed plasma. Knock-on card: MCH and MCHC are calculated from Hb, so they rise falsely too.

cues.text: The photometer cannot tell hemoglobin from anything else that blocks light. Turbidity in the lysate raises the absorbance, and the analyzer reports a falsely high hemoglobin.
The classic cause is lipemia: severe hypertriglyceridemia, or a sample drawn during an intravenous lipid infusion.

Major hyperleukocytosis with large, granular cells, as in chronic or acute myeloid leukaemia, can do it too, because the lysed white cells release their contents. Abundant monoclonal IgM or cryoglobulins can precipitate with some reagents, even when the plasma looks clear.
MCH and MCHC are calculated from the hemoglobin, so a falsely high hemoglobin drags them up as well. A very high MCHC is often the first clue.

scenes.title: Catch it, fix it, and mind the specimen source
scenes.altText: Check card: rule of three (Hct ≈ Hb × 3 ± 3) fails; MCHC very high (above about 36 g/dL in lipemic samples). Fix card: redraw away from a lipid infusion; use an optical (cell-based) Hb channel where the analyzer has one; or replace the turbid plasma and re-measure. Specimen card: capillary Hb is usually, but not always, a little higher than venous; in a large donor study most paired values differed by 1 g/dL or less; single drops can differ by more than 1.6 g/dL; wipe away the first drop. Hook answers: (1) artefact — 19.5 × 3 = 58.5, far from Hct 39%, MCHC 50; (2) a 0.6 g/dL capillary–venous gap is within the range studies report.

cues.text: Check the rule of three: hematocrit should be about three times the hemoglobin, give or take three. A turbid sample breaks the rule, and the MCHC climbs above about thirty-six grams per decilitre.
To fix it, redraw away from any lipid infusion, use an optical hemoglobin channel if the analyzer has one, or replace the turbid plasma and measure again.

Mind the specimen source too. Most studies find capillary hemoglobin a little higher than venous, but not all, and paired values usually differ by about one gram per decilitre or less. Single drops can vary, and the first drop is normally wiped away.
Back to the hook. Nineteen point five times three is far above thirty-nine, with an MCHC of fifty: an artefact. The point-six gap between finger-stick and venous fits the usual range.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “High HiCN absorbance means high hemoglobin” (✓ turbidity from lipemia, huge WBC counts or paraproteins raises absorbance; check the rule of three and MCHC); “Drabkin’s converts every hemoglobin” (✓ sulfhemoglobin is not converted); “Capillary Hb runs about 3 g/dL above venous” (✓ studies report differences mostly of about 1 g/dL or less, and the direction varies).

cues.text: Trap one: a high absorbance means a high hemoglobin. No: lipemia, a huge count of large granular white cells, or a paraprotein can raise the absorbance. Check the rule of three and the MCHC.
Trap two: Drabkin’s solution converts every hemoglobin. No: sulfhemoglobin is not converted.
Trap three: capillary hemoglobin runs three grams above venous. No: open studies report differences mostly of about one gram or less, and not always in the same direction.

props.title: ✗ “High A540 = high Hb.”
lines: ✓ Turbidity raises it; check Hb × 3 and MCHC

scenes.title: The photometer counts shadows
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “540 is HiCN’s home, and the photometer counts shadows: anything that casts one in the cuvette (fat, white-cell debris, precipitated protein) is counted as hemoglobin, while sulfhemoglobin never gets its HiCN ticket.” Tokens: 540 nm · shadows = turbidity · no ticket = sulfHb. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: five-forty is HiCN’s home, and the photometer counts shadows. Fat, white-cell debris or precipitated protein all cast one, and each is counted as hemoglobin. Sulfhemoglobin never gets its HiCN ticket.

Where it breaks: icteric plasma interferes through its colour, not a shadow; optical analyzer channels measure hemoglobin inside cells and avoid much of the turbidity; and how much interference occurs varies with the analyzer and, for white cells, with the cell type.

lines: Optical Hb channels avoid much turbidity
Effect varies by analyzer, cell type

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “HiCN at 540 nm · sulfHb not converted · turbidity reads as Hb”, “Check Hct ≈ Hb × 3 and MCHC · capillary vs venous usually ≤ ~1 g/dL, either direction”.

cues.text: In the reference method hemoglobin is read as cyanmethemoglobin at 540 nm, so anything that clouds the lysate falsely raises it, sulfhemoglobin is not converted, and finger-stick values usually differ from venous ones by about a gram or less, in either direction.

props.label: HiCN at 540 nm · sulfHb not converted · turbidity reads as Hb
Check Hb × 3 and MCHC · capillary vs venous ≈ ≤ 1 g/dL, either way

explanation.what: Plain language: the lab measures hemoglobin by turning it into one coloured compound and measuring how much light it absorbs. Anything else that blocks light makes the hemoglobin look higher than it is. Scientific terms: cyanmethemoglobin (hemiglobincyanide, HiCN), Drabkin’s solution, potassium ferricyanide, potassium cyanide, absorbance at 540 nm, sulfhemoglobin, sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS), turbidity, lipemia, hyperleukocytosis, monoclonal IgM, cryoglobulin, rule of three, optical hemoglobin channel, capillary versus venous sampling.
explanation.why: Ferricyanide oxidises hemoglobin to methemoglobin and cyanide converts it to HiCN, a single stable compound read against a standard. Particles or precipitates in the lysate add to the measured absorbance, so hemoglobin, MCH and MCHC rise falsely. Capillary samples can differ from venous ones because of collection technique and drop-to-drop variation, and possibly biology; the biological basis is still debated.
explanation.measure: HiCN read at 540 nm; oxy-, met- and carboxyhemoglobin converted, sulfhemoglobin not. Rule of three: Hct ≈ Hb × 3 ± 3. Lipemic interference is typically discovered through MCHC above about 36 g/dL (360 g/L). Capillary–venous Hb differences: mostly about 1 g/dL or less, direction varies between studies.
explanation.differs: True high Hb (Hct rises with it, MCHC normal) vs turbidity artefact (Hct does not follow, MCHC very high); HiCN-convertible derivatives vs sulfhemoglobin; capillary vs venous specimens.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: a lipemic or leukaemic sample with an implausible Hb and MCHC, the wavelength and reagent of the reference method, the derivative Drabkin’s does not convert, or a question about mixing capillary and venous results.

mnemonic.text: 540 is HiCN’s home, and the photometer counts shadows: anything that casts one in the cuvette (fat, white-cell debris, precipitated protein) is counted as hemoglobin, while sulfhemoglobin never gets its HiCN ticket.
mnemonic.explanation: Links the reading wavelength, the turbidity artefact and the non-converted derivative.
mnemonic.limitation: Icteric plasma interferes through its colour rather than turbidity; optical analyzer channels avoid much turbidity; the size of the interference varies with the analyzer and, for leukocytosis, with the cell type, so there is no single cut-off.

analogyLimitations: Cuvette and reaction drawings are schematic.
The capillary–venous range comes from published studies; individual pairs can differ more.
takeaway: In the reference method hemoglobin is read as cyanmethemoglobin at 540 nm, so anything that clouds the lysate falsely raises it, sulfhemoglobin is not converted, and finger-stick values usually differ from venous ones by about a gram or less, in either direction.

questions.stem: A milky sample from a patient receiving an intravenous lipid infusion gives Hb 19.5 g/dL, Hct 39% and MCHC 50 g/dL. What is the best next step?

options.text: Treat the Hb as a turbidity artefact: redraw away from the infusion, or use an optical Hb channel or plasma replacement
options.rationale: Correct. The rule of three fails (19.5 × 3 is far above 39) and the MCHC is implausibly high, both typical of lipemic interference.

options.text: Report the Hb and suggest polycythemia
options.rationale: Incorrect. In true polycythemia the hematocrit rises with the hemoglobin; here it does not.

options.text: Report spherocytosis because the MCHC is high
options.rationale: Incorrect. An MCHC of 50 g/dL in a lipemic sample points to falsely high Hb, not a red-cell disorder.

options.text: Re-read the same lysate at 540 nm
options.rationale: Incorrect. The turbidity is still in the lysate, so the reading stays falsely high.

questions.stem: Which hemoglobin derivative is NOT converted to hemiglobincyanide by Drabkin’s solution?

options.rationale: Correct. Sulfhemoglobin is not converted, so the HiCN method does not measure it.
Incorrect. Carboxyhemoglobin is converted and measured.
Incorrect. Methemoglobin is the intermediate that cyanide converts to HiCN.
Incorrect. Oxyhemoglobin is oxidised by ferricyanide and converted.

questions.stem: A clinic compares finger-stick Hb results with venous analyzer results from the same patients. Which statement is best supported by published comparisons?

options.text: Capillary Hb is usually a little higher than venous, but the size and direction of the difference vary, so results from the two specimen types should not be compared directly
options.rationale: Correct. Most studies find capillary Hb slightly higher, mostly by about 1 g/dL or less, but some find the reverse.

options.text: Capillary Hb is always about 3 g/dL higher than venous
options.rationale: Incorrect. Reported differences are mostly about 1 g/dL or less, and not always in the same direction.

options.text: Capillary Hb is always lower than venous
options.rationale: Incorrect. Most studies find capillary Hb higher, although some find it lower.

options.text: The two specimen types give identical results, so they can be used interchangeably
options.rationale: Incorrect. Significant differences are common, and single capillary drops can vary by more than 1.6 g/dL.

French-Speaking Cellular Haematology Group (GFHC) Review of Causes, Rising Trends and Practical Solutions. Int J Lab Hematol. 2025;47(5):798-807. doi:10.1111/ijlh.14536
references.usedFor: ICSH recommends the Drabkin (HiCN) method as reference; analyzers use non-cyanide reagents; lipemic, icteric and haemolysed plasma overestimate Hb and MCHC; redraw away from lipid infusions; IgM paraprotein and cryoglobulins precipitating with reagents despite normal plasma appearance; major hyperleukocytosis with large granular cells (CML, AML) overestimating Hb; optical Hb channels.

references.citation: Fan Y, Shen Y, Liu D, Wang Y, Cao J, Zhao B, Ma Y, Chen Z, Zhang S. Lipid Interference Flagging and Haemoglobin Correction in Lipemic Samples With a Hematology Analyzer. J Clin Lab Anal. 2026;40(12):e70223. doi:10.1002/jcla.70223
references.usedFor: Plasma turbidity falsely elevates colorimetric Hb, MCH and MCHC; detection through MCHC above about 360 g/L and failed rules of three (Hct = Hb × 3 ± 3); conventional correction by replacing turbid plasma; optical Hb unaffected by turbidity.

references.citation: Henry S, Gérard D, Salignac S, Perrin J. Optimizing the management of analytical interferences affecting red blood cells on XN-10 (Sysmex®). Int J Lab Hematol. 2022;44(6):1068-1077. doi:10.1111/ijlh.13951
references.usedFor: Recognised RBC-parameter interferences (lipemia, immunoglobulins, cryoglobulins, leukocytosis); leukocytosis threshold of 90 ×10⁹/L used in this study (another study used 100 ×10⁹/L), with the authors noting that a unique cut-off is very difficult to define because interference depends on cell type and underlying disease, not only the WBC count (evidence for register flag rv-hicn-wbc-threshold); management of interferences varies with the measurement system.

references.citation: Neufeld LM, Larson LM, Kurpad A, Mburu S, Martorell R, Brown KH. Hemoglobin concentration and anemia diagnosis in venous and capillary blood: biological basis and policy implications. Ann N Y Acad Sci. 2019;1450(1):172-189. doi:10.1111/nyas.14139
references.usedFor: Most but not all studies find capillary Hb higher than venous; differences in a large donor study mostly 1 g/dL or less; analyzer studies about 2–3% higher in capillary blood; Uttar Pradesh survey found venous higher by 0.9 g/dL; drop-to-drop variation above 1.6 g/dL; venous analyzer Hb as usual standard; HiCN as gold standard; recommendation to avoid comparing Hb estimates from venous and capillary samples.

references.citation: Krleza JL, Dorotic A, Grzunov A, Maradin M, Croatian Society of Medical Biochemistry and Laboratory Medicine. Capillary blood sampling: national recommendations on behalf of the Croatian Society of Medical Biochemistry and Laboratory Medicine. Biochem Med (Zagreb). 2015;25(3):335-358. doi:10.11613/bm.2015.034
references.usedFor: Wipe away the first capillary drop (except where a point-of-care device maker specifies otherwise); capillary haematology values can differ significantly from venous values (studies vary; CLSI GP42-A6 reports no significant difference); a cited study found capillary Hb and RBC count higher than venous (direction only; no magnitude given).

claims.text: HiCN reaction chain, Drabkin’s composition, 540 nm reading, derivatives converted and sulfhemoglobin not converted; ICSH reference method; cyanide-free analyzer reagents.
Lipemia, major hyperleukocytosis with large granular cells, IgM paraprotein and cryoglobulins falsely raise photometric Hb, MCH and MCHC.
Rule of three and MCHC above about 36 g/dL as clues; redraw away from infusion, optical Hb or plasma replacement as fixes.
Capillary Hb usually but not always higher than venous; differences mostly about 1 g/dL or less; drop variation; wipe the first drop.
claims.note: Contradicts the reviewer’s ~3 g/dL (register flag rv-capillary-venous-hb-gap).

claims.text: Reviewer’s WBC >30 ×10⁹/L threshold for HiCN interference; capillary RBC exceeding venous by ~0.5 ×10¹²/L.
claims.note: Not taught as facts; no open source read in this session gives these figures. Krleza 2015 supports only the direction of the RBC difference (capillary higher), not the ~0.5 ×10¹²/L magnitude.

claims.text: Scenario invented; cuvette and reaction drawings schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 31 Hit 12 states capillary Hb exceeds venous by ~3 g/dL. Neufeld 2019 reports that most, but not all, studies find capillary Hb higher: in a large donor study most paired values differed by 1 g/dL or less, analyzer-based studies found capillary about 2–3% higher, and a large survey found venous higher by a mean 0.9 g/dL (register flag rv-capillary-venous-hb-gap). The RBC ~0.5 ×10¹²/L magnitude was not verified (Krleza 2015 supports only the direction).

Ch. 31 Exam Trap 2 gives WBC >30 ×10⁹/L as the level at which leukocytosis raises HiCN absorbance. Girard 2025 describes major hyperleukocytosis with large granular cells, and Henry 2022 used 90 ×10⁹/L while noting that a unique cut-off is very difficult to define because interference depends on cell type; the threshold is not taught (register flag rv-hicn-wbc-threshold).
